6. A necessary condition on every successful compiler

There is a general constraint that helps distinguish a genuine protected transition from a merely correct noiseless one.

Restrict to a unitary target  $\mathcal U$ . Let  $\mathcal P_t$  be the noiseless compiled prefix through layer  $t$ , including the input encoding and honest classical records. Let  $\mathcal S_t$  be the remaining circuit followed by the specified output recovery.

The requested guarantee, applied to a fault only at time  $t$ , requires

 $\left\|
\mathcal S_t\circ\mathcal F_A\circ\mathcal P_t
-\mathcal U
\right\|_\diamond
\le\epsilon
\tag{12}$ for every allowed fault on every allowed set  $A$ .

Consequently

 $\mathcal R_t=\mathcal U^{-1}\circ\mathcal S_t$ is a mathematical recovery satisfying

 $\left\|
\mathcal R_t\circ\mathcal F_A\circ\mathcal P_t
-\operatorname{id}
\right\|_\diamond
\le\epsilon.
\tag{13}$ Therefore every intermediate representation must retain the logical quantum information after every allowed erasure, not only the endpoint codes.

If an allowed erasure makes an initially maximally entangled logical qubit separable from all remaining honest systems, no suffix can repair that loss. Its unhalved diamond distance from the intended unitary is at least  $1$ .

This rules out an exposed small quantum carrier when its location is legally targetable. It does not rule out jointly encoded intermediate states, private-location constructions that actually establish their secrecy contract, or other architectures satisfying (13). It is not a general no-go theorem.
